questions.prompt: Vatican II's Sacrosanctum Concilium 36 states that 'the use of the Latin language... is to be preserved' in which context?
choices: The Latin rites, even while permitting the vernacular's wider use in the liturgy
Only in private prayer, never in any public liturgy
Only for the Extraordinary Form, with no bearing on the ordinary liturgy
Nowhere -- the document abolishes Latin's liturgical use entirely
questions.correctAnswer: The Latin rites, even while permitting the vernacular's wider use in the liturgy
questions.explanation: The council that authorized the vernacular's expanded use is the same council that explicitly preserved Latin's place -- these are not opposed decisions but two parts of one balanced reform, easily lost when only one half is remembered.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same document that expanded the vernacular's use also abolished Latin, or held both together.

questions.prompt: True or False: The official reference edition (editio typica) of the Roman Missal and other liturgical books remains published in Latin, even in dioceses that celebrate exclusively in the vernacular.
questions.explanation: True. Every vernacular translation is measured against this Latin reference text, which is why translation revisions are checked against the editio typica rather than against an earlier vernacular version -- Latin remains the standard against which fidelity is judged.
questions.hint: Ask what a vernacular translation is actually checked against for accuracy.

questions.prompt: Beyond the liturgy, in what other capacity does the Holy See continue to use Latin as an official language?
choices: The Code of Canon Law and many formal Vatican documents are promulgated with Latin as their official text
Latin has no remaining official use anywhere outside the liturgy
Latin is used only for internal Vatican correspondence, never for published law
Latin was replaced by Italian as the Holy See's official legal language
questions.correctAnswer: The Code of Canon Law and many formal Vatican documents are promulgated with Latin as their official text
questions.explanation: Canon law's official text remains Latin, and many papal documents carry a Latin title and an authoritative Latin text alongside vernacular translations -- Latin's role as the Church's working legal and administrative language continues well beyond the sanctuary.
questions.hint: Ask what legal text this database has cited by its Latin title throughout this whole topic.

questions.prompt: A language preserved specifically because it does not change with everyday usage, keeping doctrinal formulas stable across centuries and translations, is sometimes called a 'sacred' or ____ language.
questions.explanation: A language no longer spoken as anyone's native tongue stops shifting in the way living vernaculars constantly do -- which is part of why the Church has valued Latin's very fixedness as an asset for doctrinal precision, not merely kept it out of custom.
questions.hint: The word describes the language's specific role in worship, distinct from a 'dead' language spoken nowhere.

questions.prompt: True or False: Everything covered across this entire topic -- vocabulary, prayers, Mass responses, magisterial texts, hymns, Scripture, patristic Latin and grammar -- serves one underlying purpose: enabling direct access to the Church's own words, rather than only a translation of them.

Every level, from 'Agnus Dei' meaning 'Lamb of God' to a purpose clause in a Collect, has aimed at the same thing: letting the reader meet the Church's prayer, teaching and Scripture in the words she herself actually uses, not only in someone else's rendering of them.

questions.prompt: Reading 'Ite, missa est' with the grammar covered earlier in this topic, the Mass's own name emerges from which single word?
choices: 'Missa' -- the passive participle of 'mittere,' to send
'Ite' -- the imperative meaning 'go'
'Est' -- the verb 'to be'
None of these three words relates to the Mass's name
questions.correctAnswer: 'Missa' -- the passive participle of 'mittere,' to send
questions.explanation: This draws directly on level 9's own material: 'missa,' sent, gives the Mass its name because the dismissal -- being sent out to live what was just celebrated -- was considered the defining final act of the whole liturgy.
questions.hint: The dismissal word 'missa' -- being sent out -- literally names the whole Mass after its final act.

questions.prompt: Considering this topic as a whole, why does the Church maintain Latin's place rather than simply completing a full transition to the vernacular everywhere?

Because the vernacular is considered doctrinally inferior to Latin

questions.correctAnswer: Latin provides a stable, precise, and unifying reference across the whole Latin Church, even while the vernacular carries the ordinary daily experience of worship for most of the faithful
questions.explanation: Both things are true at once, exactly as Sacrosanctum Concilium held them together at the start of this level: the vernacular is not a lesser accommodation, and Latin is not a relic being merely tolerated -- each serves a real and different purpose in the Church's actual life.
